case_prompt: Patient is a 40-year-old man with a history of reactive arthritis, Graves’ disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, mitral valve prolapse, and Gilbert’s disease who presented with one month of progressive jaundice, fatigue, lightheadedness, and exertional dyspnea. He described dark urine and dark brown to black stools. He denied fevers, chills, or recent transfusions and had no history of hepatitis, alcohol or intravenous drug use. His medications included etanercept, methimazole, niacin, and aspirin; he had discontinued metformin and pioglitazone more than one month before symptom onset. Family history was notable for autoimmune hemolytic anemia in his mother and anemia of unknown cause in his maternal grandmother. On examination, he was jaundiced with scleral icterus; vital signs showed heart rate 102 beats per minute and normal blood pressure, respiratory rate, and temperature. There was no lymphadenopathy. The thyroid gland was non-tender without enlargement or exophthalmos. Cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed mild hepatomegaly without splenomegaly. A vesiculobullous rash was present on the plantar surface of the right foot. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 5.8 g/dL, hematocrit 18.7%, MCV 107.5 fL, reticulocyte count 23.4%, total bilirubin 13.6 mg/dL (direct 0.6 mg/dL), LDH 369 U/L, and undetectable haptoglobin. Hepatitis serologies, antinuclear antibody, cold agglutinins, cryoglobulins, and HIV were negative. Coagulation studies were within normal limits. Peripheral smear showed spherocytes and bite cells without schistocytes. Direct antiglobulin test was positive for IgG and negative for C3; indirect antiglobulin test was negative. G6PD level and thyroid-stimulating hormone were normal. Lumbar spine radiographs showed sacroiliac joint ankylosis. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed probable anterior mediastinal enlargement, mild splenomegaly, and multiple small hypodensities in the liver and kidneys.

diagnostic_reasoning: 1. Hereditary spherocytosis considered — “the patient did not have a history of chronic anemia, which was against the diagnosis of hereditary spherocytosis.” 2. Metformin-induced hemolytic anemia considered — “our patient had stopped metformin at least a month before his symptoms developed, so this was very unlikely.” 3. Etanercept-associated cold agglutinin disease considered — “…cold agglutinin disease is associated with IgM antibodies…our patient’s cold agglutinin screen was negative.” 4. Drug-induced hemolysis from other medications considered — “None of his other medications have been reported to cause hemolytic anemia.” 5. Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia favored — “The leading diagnosis was therefore WAIHA.”

selection.screen_reason: Hemolytic anemia with spherocytes and an IgG-positive direct antiglobulin test in a man with autoimmune history gives warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
selection.second_look_note: Reliable account of jaundice and dark urine, drug exposures and a mother with autoimmune hemolytic anemia frames a hemolysis workup that the IgG-positive direct antiglobulin test decides.
